title: Improving Mathematics Performance in Algebra by Using A Videogame Style Points-Based Feedback System
venue: International Journal of Social Science and Economic Research
extended_summary:
This paper asks whether adding videogame-style points to mathematics practice can improve students’ algebra performance. It builds on the authors’ prior work showing that points for correct answers improved elementary students’ math performance, and tests whether the same effect appears with older students.

The intervention compared two versions of software presenting 20 algebra mixture problems. In the treatment condition, students received feedback on correctness plus 100 points for each correct answer and a running cumulative total. In the control condition, students only received correctness feedback and no points. The problems were delivered via software and were used as practice/homework-like tasks rather than direct instruction.

The study involved 28 middle and high school students who had taken Algebra 1. Participants were randomly assigned individually to the points or no-points version and completed the task in a one-day session. The authors report that students receiving points scored significantly higher, averaging 16.3 correct answers versus 11.1 in the control group, a difference of about 47%.

The paper concludes that a simple points-based feedback system can motivate students to solve more problems correctly and may provide an easy, low-cost way to improve mathematics performance. The authors suggest the approach may generalize across age groups and could be extended to classroom grading or self-directed learning contexts, though they note that effects may differ when students are learning intrinsically interesting material.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a small quasi-experimental/experimental comparison with random assignment to conditions, but the paper reports limited methodological detail and only one small sample from middle/high school students. It is peer-reviewed, but it does not meet strong RCT criteria for high credibility due to small sample size and limited outcome reporting.
impact_tier_rationale: The reported gain is large in the primary math outcome (about 47% higher performance), which suggests meaningful immediate impact for a middle/high school algebra practice task. However, the evidence comes from a very small sample and a narrow task, so the broader generalization remains modest.

interventions.use_case: videogame-style points-based feedback delivered through software for solving algebra mixture problems, with immediate correctness feedback and cumulative point totals

finding.finding_summary: Middle and high school students (n=28) who received videogame-style points for each correct algebra answer scored substantially higher on a 20-item mixture-problems test than students who only received correctness feedback. Mean performance was 16.3/20 with points versus 11.1/20 without points, a statistically significant difference of about 47% (t=3.18, df=26, p<.005).
finding.measure: Number of correct answers on 20 algebra mixture problems (all-or-none scoring)

finding.finding_summary: The intervention was designed to increase motivation by awarding 100 points per correct response and showing cumulative totals, and the authors interpret the higher algebra scores as evidence that the points motivated participants to perform better. No direct motivation scale was reported in the main result for this study, so the evidence is indirect but consistent with improved engagement/motivation during problem solving.
finding.measure: Motivationally framed points-based feedback during problem solving; no direct motivation measure reported in the key result
